book.title: The AI Ready School
book.author: Stephen R. Jordan

name: Arts, Music, Physical Education, and Health
blurb: In a small study in Turkey, one class of sixth graders took a visual arts course that used AI tools, while a similar class took the same course without them. By the end, the students who used AI held more positive attitudes toward art and scored higher on the course outcomes (Kara, 2025).
title: Arts, Music, Physical Education, and Health

papers.title: Innovations of music and aesthetic education courses using intelligent technologies
papers.caveat: Music schools, not general classrooms; no randomized control.
papers.finding: 343 elementary, middle, and high school students in Beijing music schools improved instrument proficiency with intelligent technologies; gains varied by instrument.

papers.why: Only K-12 visual arts study found.
papers.title: The Effect of Artificial Intelligence Applications in 6th Grade Visual Arts Course on Student Attitudes and Course Outcomes
papers.venue: International Journal of Modern Education Studies
papers.finding: Quasi-experiment with 40 sixth graders in Turkey: AI-supported visual arts lessons raised attitudes and course outcome scores over a control group.

papers.why: Only review found for AI in PE.
papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Physical Education: A Systematic Review of Personalized Learning, Assessment, and Performance Analytics
papers.caveat: Mixed K-12 and higher ed; low-profile journal; mostly short studies.
papers.finding: Review of 87 studies (K-12 and higher education): AI in PE linked to engagement and more consistent assessment; concerns about data privacy, bias, and weak teacher-AI frameworks.

children.name: The Authorship Rule
children.blurb: The Authorship Rule is a clear school-wide agreement that students must make their own creative work and disclose any AI help they use.

children.name: Music Practice and Composition
children.blurb: This idea is about using AI in music education for practice, theory drills and composition feedback while keeping the teacher and student in charge of creative decisions.

children.name: Art History and Portfolios
children.blurb: This idea uses AI to help teachers open conversations about art history and to help students build portfolios that show growth.

children.name: Drama and Performance
children.blurb: Drama and performance can use AI as a rehearsal partner and as a drafting assistant for production tasks, while keeping the creative work with students and the director.

children.name: Physical Education: Planning and Adaptation
children.blurb: This idea is that AI can help physical education teachers generate and adapt activity options, station rotations, and personal fitness plan drafts for students with different skills, abilities, and interests.

children.name: Form Feedback From Video
children.blurb: Form feedback from video means students record their own movement, such as a basketball shot or running stride, then watch it back to compare with good form.

children.name: Health Education
children.blurb: Health education with AI can give students a private way to ask sensitive health questions through a school configured tool that draws only on approved materials.

children.name: Keeping Health Information Out of AI Tools
children.blurb: Student health information is among the most sensitive records a school holds, and a teacher who types a student's diagnosis, medication or injury into a general chat tool has handed that record to a company the school has no agreement with.

children.name: Teaching Students About AI Art
children.blurb: Teaching students about AI art means helping them examine images, music and video made by machines rather than training them to produce such work.

children.name: Media Arts, Photography, and Film
children.blurb: Media arts, photography, and film classes are places where AI features are already built into digital tools, from photo editing that removes objects or changes backgrounds to video editors that generate captions, suggest cuts, or create effects.

children.name: Arts and PE for Students With Disabilities
children.blurb: This idea is that AI tools can help students with disabilities take part in arts, music, physical education, and health by offering new ways to create and move, such as voice or eye controlled digital art or audio feedback for music composition.

children.name: Planning and Feedback for Arts and PE Teachers
children.blurb: This idea is that AI can serve as a planning partner for arts, music, PE, and health teachers who often have no colleague in their subject nearby.

sections.body: This section covers the parts of school life where the student's own hands, voice, and body are the point, including arts, music, physical education, and health. The book describes AI here as a brainstorm partner, a practice aid, and a planning tool for teachers, never the maker of student work. It notes a small study in Turkey where sixth graders in a visual arts course using AI held more positive attitudes toward art and scored higher on course outcomes, while cautioning that the study involved only 40 students at one school and proves little on its own. A review of 87 studies of AI in physical education found better engagement and more consistent assessment alongside real concerns about privacy and bias. The chapter also covers the authorship rule, music practice and composition, art history and portfolios, drama and performance, PE planning and feedback, health education, and the special care student health information requires.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The book finds that AI can play a useful role even in the most human of subjects, and that research in these areas is thinner than in reading or math, with most ideas being sensible practices rather than proven methods. The studies that exist are small and mostly not randomized, though they point in encouraging directions, so teachers should treat these ideas as worth trying carefully, not as sure bets. What does not work is the generated masterpiece, where a student submits a striking image or song made entirely by AI and the teacher either misses it or has no rule to point to, after which other students follow and the program ends up grading machine work. The rule the book holds to is that AI is never the maker of student work, backed by a written authorship rule shared with students and families and a clear instruction that health information never goes into general AI tools. A general AI policy is not enough on its own, and what counts is specific rules that teachers in these subjects actually follow.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages move from the core authorship rule outward into each subject and then into the safeguards. A teacher would go to The Authorship Rule for the line itself, to Music Practice and Composition, Art History and Portfolios, Drama and Performance, and Media Arts, Photography, and Film for how the rule plays out in each creative subject, and to Teaching Students About AI Art for helping students see where that line sits. For movement and wellbeing, Physical Education: Planning and Adaptation, Form Feedback From Video, and Health Education cover practice and planning, while Keeping Health Information Out of AI Tools holds the privacy rule that health details never enter general AI tools. Leaders and parents would go to Arts and PE for Students With Disabilities for inclusion, to Planning and Feedback for Arts and PE Teachers for the teacher-facing planning and feedback work, and to the board question and the Thirty Day Move, which ask for a written authorship rule shared with families and a tested crisis routing record before any student sees a health question tool.
